title: Larkspur Gateway & Private Connectivity Walkthrough
summary: Discovery focused on Larkspur's requirements for a private deployment of Redwood Inference inside their AWS accounts. Key concerns: cross-account routing, CIDR conflicts, egress controls through corporate firewall, EU data residency, and the integration of KMS and audit logs. SE walked through options: VPC peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink endpoints; agreed next steps include an architecture whiteboard, port/endpoint list, and a hands-on workshop to test connectivity.
next_steps: Redwood to send VPC connectivity checklist and minimal port list (Jordan)

Schedule 90-min technical workshop with customer's network and security (Marcus/Jordan)
Share Redwood security brief and SOC 2 audit page (Aisha)
Customer to provide expected QPS and peak token rates for pilot (Evan)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 15:00 EDT
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Kapoor (Redwood CSM); Nina Rao (Head of Platform - Larkspur), Tom Hernandez (Network), Priya Singh (Security), Evan Cole (SRE)

Summary auto-note (auto): private deployment networking deep dive, route options, region requirements.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan with Redwood Inference. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Nina: Nina here.
[00:13] Tom: Tom, hi.
[00:15] Priya: Priya here.
[00:18] Evan: Evan on the call.
[00:20] Marcus: Marcus, se from Redwood. Glad to dig into the VPC stuff.

[00:35] Jordan: High level, Larkspur flagged that you want the inference runtime to live in your AWS accounts with private connectivity into your services, is that correct?
[00:42] Nina: Yeah, correct. We want no public internet egress for inference. Must be internal-only, and EU data must remain in eu-west-1.
[00:50] Jordan: Great. Marcus, want to walk through the connectivity options?

[01:02] Marcus: Sure. There are three common patterns: classical cross-account VPC peering, Transit Gateway (TGW) attachments, and PrivateLink / AWS Private endpoints. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:16] Tom: We're leaning away from peptide — sorry, peering — if we have lots of accounts. We use a hub-and-spoke via TGW already for most infra.
[01:24] Marcus: That helps. TGW gives a single routing hub and supports route propagation; but we need to watch CIDR overlap and scale of route tables. PrivateLink is more like a service fronted with an ENI in your VPC that talks only to Redwood's service endpoint — less routing complexity, but you need NLBs and ENIs per AZ.
[01:45] Priya: For security, PrivateLink looks good because it avoids route propagation across many accounts. But our egress policy requires all external traffic hit our corporate firewall / proxy. If Redwood still needs to pull updates or call telemetry endpoints, can that be routed through our egress?
[02:05] Marcus: Yes, you can either force Redwood outbound through your NAT/gateway by keeping connections initiated from inside the VPC to the service endpoint, or configure TGW to send egress to a centralized NAT. There's a nuance: if Redwood's runtime needs to reach S3 for model artifacts, we recommend using an S3 VPC endpoint so that does not traverse the public net.
[02:28] Tom: We're concerned about overlapping CIDRs — many of our product VPCs are /16s. What's Redwood's expectation for IP space?
[02:38] Marcus: For a Private deployment we'd ask for a non-overlapping /20 per Redwood worker subnet per AZ ideally. If that's impossible we can use NAT'd private link or host the Redwood runtime in a dedicated account and use interface endpoints. NAT'ing works but adds SNAT complexity and traceability issues.
[02:56] Nina: What about cross-region? We must keep EU inference in eu-west-1 and US in us-east-1. We don't want data egress between regions.
[03:06] Marcus: That's straightforward — deployments are region-bound. We can provision separate private endpoints or TGW attachments per region. For model syncs we support regional model pinning so data and model downloads remain region-local.
[03:22] Evan: How do we handle audit logs and KMS? Our security team insists on customer-managed keys and full access logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:33] Marcus: Redwood Private supports integrating with your KMS for encryption-at-rest. For audit logs, we can deliver CloudTrail events and application-level request logs to an S3 bucket in your account or forward via Kinesis to your SIEM. We'll need IAM roles and an S3 bucket policy.
[03:48] Priya: Who owns the IAM roles? We prefer to own role definitions in our account and allow Redwood to assume them.
[03:56] Marcus: That's our normal pattern: customer creates roles with a trust policy that allows Redwood's service principal or account to assume them with limited permissions. We'll provide the exact least-privilege policy.
[04:07] Jordan: Quick question about TLS and mutual auth. Do you support mTLS for control plane connections?
[04:14] Marcus: Currently we support TLS with customer-resolvable certs; mTLS is available as an enterprise option for private deployments. We can also front the service with PrivateLink + client certs if you want mutual auth at the endpoint.
[04:28] Tom: What ports do we need to open? Corporate gets twitchy about lists.
[04:33] Marcus: We'll provide a minimal port list. Typically: 443 TCP for API/control, ephemeral ports for internal worker-to-worker (we can restrict or NAT them), and optional 22 only if you want SSH for troubleshooting which we avoid. Also port 443 for S3 endpoints if using VPC endpoints. We'll send a concrete checklist.
[04:52] Nina: For initial pilot, we want small scale and strict controls. Maybe a single AZ in eu-west-1 and one US AZ. We want to simulate peak traffic. Evan will share expected QPS.
[05:05] Evan: We're expecting about 60 concurrent open requests with bursts to 300 rps and average token rates about 150 tokens per request. That's pilot numbers, could grow.
[05:17] Marcus: Good — that helps sizing. For those numbers we recommend starting on two c4-equivalent GPU nodes in the region or a dedicated small pool; we'll share recommended sizing table.
[05:30] Priya: On compliance, we need SOC 2 and penetration test artifacts and data residency proof. Also endpoint auditing.
[05:38] Aisha: We'll send the SOC 2 summary and our security brief after the call, and a link to our compliance portal. The SOC report requires an NDA to share full docs — we'll include directions.
[05:48] Tom: If we do TGW, any limitations with route table size or number of attachments we should know?
[05:54] Marcus: TGW route tables can get large; for scale we isolate Redwood subnets in their own attachment with dedicated route table entries. If you already have a TGW policy that blocks route propagation from third-party accounts, we can work with you to create scoped route maps. Also, TGW supports route propagation from VPN or DX if you have on-prem.
[06:14] Nina: On the note of on-prem, we have a backup lab on-prem that may need to talk to the inference services over Direct Connect. Is that supported?
[06:21] Marcus: Yes, as long as route propagation and security rules allow it. We'll coordinate BGP prefixes — but prefer to avoid overlapping on-prem IPs with worker subnets.
[06:33] Tom: Any gotchas around Security Groups? We use default deny and explicit SG rules.
[06:38] Marcus: We'll want to document required SGs. Typically Redwood will require an SG that allows inbound from your application subnets on the worker API port and allows outbound to S3 endpoints and telemetry endpoints. We'll provide exact SG templates.
[06:54] Jordan: Let's talk timeline: what's needed to get a pilot in two weeks?
[06:58] Nina: Two weeks is aggressive but possible if we get the connectivity checklist and a short workshop.
[07:05] Marcus: We'll aim to run a 90-minute lab where we create the endpoint, test routing, verify S3 access via endpoint, and validate KMS access. That usually surfaces most friction points.
[07:17] Priya: We'll need Aisha's security brief before workshop.
[07:20] Aisha: Yes, I'll post that right after the call.

Misc notes: occasional transcription glitches — Redwood mis-transcribed as 'Red would' in one moment, 'PrivateLink' heard as 'private-ling' in 1 place.

[33:45] Jordan: Recap — Jordan to send connectivity checklist and port list; Marcus to prepare workshop and Terraform examples; Tom to give account IDs + CIDR ranges; Priya to outline KMS/SIEM requirements; Evan to share QPS numbers.
[34:05] Nina: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[34:10] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up via email and put calendar invite for the workshop.
[34:15] Marcus: Thanks all.
